title: Implement cross-platform abstraction layer
description:
Create the abstraction layer that hides platform differences for common operations. This layer allows core logic to be platform-agnostic while backends provide platform-specific implementations.

## Abstractions Needed

### Display/Screen Abstraction
- Enumerate displays
- Get display geometry (bounds, DPI)
- Detect display changes
- Platform: Win32/DXGI, AppKit/CGDisplay, X11/RANDR

### Window Abstraction (for wallpaper window)
- Create window at specific level
- Set window geometry
- Render to window
- Platform: Win32/DWM, NSWindow, X11/XCB

### System Events
- Sleep/wake notifications
- Display connect/disconnect
- Power state changes
- Platform: Win32 messages, NSNotification, udev/DBus

### File System
- Config file location (AppData, Library, .config)
- Log file location
- Temp file handling
- Platform: SHGetKnownFolderPath, NSSearchPathForDirectoriesInDomains, XDG

## Design Pattern
Trait/interface per abstraction with platform-specific implementations. Factory function returns appropriate implementation based on compile target.

## Testing Strategy
Mock implementations for unit testing core logic without platform dependencies.

title: Implement startup at login functionality
description:
Allow users to configure the application to launch automatically at system login. Platform-specific implementation required.

## User Setting
Settings window checkbox: "Launch at login"
When enabled: App starts minimized to tray on login

## Windows Implementation
Registry-based:
```
HKEY_CURRENT_USER\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run
Key: Micround
Value: "C:\Path\To\micround.exe" --minimized
```

Or via Task Scheduler for more control.

## macOS Implementation
Modern approach (macOS 13+):
```swift
SMAppService.mainApp.register()
```

Legacy approach:
- LaunchAgent plist in ~/Library/LaunchAgents/
- com.example.micround.plist

## Linux Implementation
XDG autostart:
```
~/.config/autostart/micround.desktop
```

Desktop file contents:
```ini
[Desktop Entry]
Type=Application
Name=Micround
Exec=/path/to/micround --minimized
Hidden=false
```

## Implementation Notes
- Enable/disable should be idempotent
- Check current state before modifying
- Handle errors gracefully (permissions, etc.)
- --minimized flag: Start directly to tray

## Testing
- Enable autostart, log out/in, verify
- Disable autostart, log out/in, verify not running
- Test on each platform

title: Implement geometric transforms (rotation and flip)
description:
Implement rotation (90° increments) and flip (horizontal/vertical) transforms for frames. Essential for correcting camera orientation mismatches and mirror effects from certain optics.

## Supported Transforms
- Rotation: 0°, 90°, 180°, 270° (clockwise)
- Horizontal flip (mirror)
- Vertical flip
- Any combination of the above

## Implementation Approach
### Simple Method (CPU)
- Rotation: Transpose + flip (90° = transpose + flip horizontal)
- Flip: Reverse row/column order
- Memory layout matters for cache efficiency

### GPU Method
- Texture coordinate transformation
- Single draw with transformed UV coordinates
- Rotation + flip combined in one pass

## Transform Order
When multiple transforms are applied:
1. Flip (if any)
2. Rotate (if any)
3. Scale (separate operation)

Document and enforce consistent ordering.

## Performance
- 90°/270° rotation changes buffer dimensions
- 180° rotation and flips can be done in-place
- GPU path should be negligible cost
- CPU path: 1080p transform <5ms

## Why Users Need This
- USB microscopes often mount at odd angles
- Some optics produce mirrored images
- User may want to match physical orientation to screen
- Rotation at capture level wastes bandwidth (software cheaper)

## Testing
- All 8 combinations (4 rotations × 2 flip states)
- Verify no off-by-one errors at edges
- Visual inspection with test patterns
- Round-trip test: rotate 4× = identity

title: Performance optimization pass
description:
After features are implemented and working, systematically optimize to meet performance targets. Don't optimize prematurely, but don't ship without meeting targets.

## Performance Targets (from requirements)
- End-to-end latency: ≤100ms (p95)
- CPU usage: ≤10% (idle desktop, feed running)
- GPU usage: ≤15%
- Memory: ≤200MB resident
- Frame rate: ≥24fps sustained

## Optimization Process

### 1. Establish Baseline
- Run latency measurement tooling
- Record CPU/GPU/memory metrics
- Identify current performance vs. targets

### 2. Profile to Find Bottlenecks
Don't guess - measure:
- CPU profiler: Where is time spent?
- GPU profiler: Shader costs, draw calls
- Memory profiler: Allocations per frame?
- Frame timing: Which stage is slowest?

### 3. Optimize Highest-Impact Items First
Common optimization opportunities:
- Reduce memory allocations (use pools)
- Minimize CPU↔GPU data transfer
- Use hardware decode for MJPEG
- Reduce draw calls
- Cache computed values

### 4. Verify Improvements
After each change:
- Re-run benchmarks
- Confirm improvement
- Check for regressions elsewhere
- Update baseline

### 5. Document Final Performance
Record achieved performance:
- Latency distribution (p50, p95, p99)
- Resource usage over time
- Test hardware specs
- Known limitations

## When to Stop
Stop optimizing when:
- All targets are met with margin
- Further optimization has diminishing returns
- Optimization would complicate code significantly

## Anti-Patterns to Avoid
- Optimizing before profiling (guessing)
- Micro-optimizing non-bottlenecks
- Breaking code clarity for tiny gains
- Ignoring thermal behavior (laptop throttling)

title: Build latency measurement tooling
description:
Create tooling to measure end-to-end latency from camera to display. Essential for validating the <100ms latency requirement with objective data.

## Latency Definition
End-to-end latency: Time from photons hitting camera sensor to photons leaving display.

## Measurement Approach

### Internal Instrumentation
Each frame carries timestamps:
- t0: Frame captured (camera callback entry)
- t1: Decode complete
- t2: Processing complete
- t3: Submitted to render
- t4: Presented (vsync or present complete)

Internal latency = t4 - t0 (excludes sensor and display latency)

### External Measurement (Ground Truth)
Physical setup:
1. Display shows millisecond counter
2. High-speed camera records display
3. Microscope camera pointed at same counter
4. Measure delay between original and microscope display

This captures true end-to-end including sensor and display.

## Internal Metrics API
```
struct FrameMetrics {
    sequence: u64,
    capture_time: Instant,
    decode_time: Instant,
    process_time: Instant,
    render_time: Instant,
}

fn get_latency_histogram() -> LatencyHistogram
fn get_recent_metrics(count: usize) -> Vec<FrameMetrics>
```

## Latency Histogram
Track distribution:
- Buckets: 0-20ms, 20-40ms, 40-60ms, 60-80ms, 80-100ms, 100ms+
- p50, p95, p99 percentiles
- Max observed

## Test Mode
Debug/test mode enables:
- Overlay showing live latency
- Latency logging to file
- Automated histogram generation

## Acceptance Test
Automated test:
1. Run with simulated camera (known timing)
2. Collect latency metrics for 1 hour
3. Assert: p95 < 100ms, p50 < 80ms

## Reporting
Latency report includes:
- Histogram visualization
- Percentile summary
- Comparison to target
- Outlier analysis

title: Verify no-network and no-recording privacy guarantees
description:
Audit and verify that the application makes no network connections and does not record video data to disk. These are core privacy promises that must be objectively verifiable.

## No Network Verification

### Code Audit
- Search for networking APIs: socket, connect, HTTP, etc.
- Verify no telemetry/analytics code
- Verify no update checking over network
- Verify no crash reporting that phones home

### Runtime Verification
- Monitor application with network tools
- Windows: Wireshark, netstat, Resource Monitor
- macOS: Little Snitch, lsof, nettop
- Linux: tcpdump, netstat, ss

### Automated Test
```
1. Block all network access (firewall rule)
2. Run application for 1 hour
3. Verify no network error handling triggered
4. Verify application functions normally
```

## No Recording Verification

### Code Audit
- Search for file writing APIs with video extensions
- Verify frame data never written to disk
- Verify frame buffers don't persist beyond processing
- Exception: Explicit snapshot feature (user-initiated only)

### Runtime Verification
- Monitor filesystem writes during operation
- Windows: Process Monitor (ProcMon)
- macOS: fs_usage
- Linux: strace, inotify

### Automated Test
```
1. Start with empty temp/cache directories
2. Run feed for 1 hour
3. Verify no video files created
4. Only allowed: logs, config, explicit snapshots
```

## Documentation
- Document privacy guarantees clearly
- Explain what data IS stored (config, logs)
- Explain what data IS NOT stored (video)
- Provide verification instructions for skeptical users

## Testing
- Run verification on each platform
- Run before each release
- Document results

title: Implement V4L2 camera capture on Linux
description:
Implement camera capture using Video4Linux2 (V4L2), the standard Linux video capture API. Most USB cameras present as V4L2 devices.

## V4L2 Capture Flow
1. Open device: open("/dev/video0", O_RDWR)
2. Query capabilities: ioctl(VIDIOC_QUERYCAP)
3. Set format: ioctl(VIDIOC_S_FMT)
4. Request buffers: ioctl(VIDIOC_REQBUFS)
5. Map buffers: mmap() for each buffer
6. Queue buffers: ioctl(VIDIOC_QBUF)
7. Start stream: ioctl(VIDIOC_STREAMON)
8. Capture loop: poll(), ioctl(VIDIOC_DQBUF), process, VIDIOC_QBUF
9. Stop: ioctl(VIDIOC_STREAMOFF)
10. Cleanup: munmap(), close()

## Device Enumeration
```c
// List /dev/video* devices
// For each, query VIDIOC_QUERYCAP
// Filter for V4L2_CAP_VIDEO_CAPTURE capability
```

## Format Negotiation
```c
struct v4l2_format fmt;
fmt.type = V4L2_BUF_TYPE_VIDEO_CAPTURE;
fmt.fmt.pix.width = desired_width;
fmt.fmt.pix.height = desired_height;
fmt.fmt.pix.pixelformat = V4L2_PIX_FMT_MJPEG; // or YUYV
ioctl(fd, VIDIOC_S_FMT, &fmt);
// Check actual format in fmt after call
```

## Buffer Strategy
- Use memory-mapped buffers (MMAP)
- Request 2-4 buffers
- Keeps pipeline full while processing

## Hot-Plug Detection
- udev for device events
- inotify on /dev/video*
- Or periodic enumeration (less responsive)

## Permissions
Device access requires:
- User in 'video' group, OR
- udev rule for specific device, OR
- Run as root (not recommended)

## Testing
- Multiple camera types
- Various resolutions
- Hot-plug detection
- Permission scenarios

title: Implement pause/freeze frame functionality
description:
Allow users to freeze the current frame while capture continues in the background. Useful for examining a moment without stopping the feed.

## Behavior
- Pause: Display freezes on current frame
- Capture continues (camera stays open)
- Resume: Display updates with live feed again
- No frame gap on resume (immediately current)

## Implementation
```
On Pause:
1. Copy current processed frame to 'frozen' buffer
2. Set display mode to 'frozen'
3. Render pipeline shows frozen frame
4. Capture pipeline continues (discard frames to frozen buffer)

On Resume:
1. Clear display mode flag
2. Next frame goes to display
3. Discard frozen buffer (or keep for snapshot)
```

## UI Integration
- Tray menu: "Pause" / "Resume" toggle
- Keyboard shortcut: Configurable (suggest Space or P)
- Status indicator: Tray tooltip shows "Paused"
- Optional: Overlay text "PAUSED" (subtle)

## Use Cases
- Examine interesting moment
- Take notes without motion
- Step away briefly without missing content (debatable)

## Edge Cases
- Pause while already paused: No-op
- Camera disconnect while paused: Show frozen frame, normal reconnect flow
- Snapshot while paused: Capture frozen frame

## Testing
- Pause and resume multiple times
- Verify no memory leak (frozen buffer management)
- Verify capture continues (reconnect test)
- Verify snapshot works while paused

title: Implement camera reconnection logic
description:
Automatically reconnect to the camera when it becomes available again after disconnection. Essential for day-30 reliability where USB devices may be bumped.

## Reconnection Flow
```
Camera Disconnected
       │
       ▼
┌──────────────────┐
│ Freeze last frame │
│ Show overlay      │
└────────┬─────────┘
         │
         ▼
┌──────────────────┐     device appears
│   Poll for device │────────────────────┐
│   (every 2 sec)   │                    │
└────────┬─────────┘                     │
         │ timeout (30 sec)              │
         ▼                               ▼
┌──────────────────┐          ┌──────────────────┐
│ Show fallback     │          │ Attempt reconnect │
│ wallpaper         │          └────────┬─────────┘
│ Notify user       │                   │
└──────────────────┘           success  │  failure
                                        ▼         │
                               ┌────────────┐     │
                               │ Resume feed │◄────┘ (retry)
                               └────────────┘
```

## Device Matching
Match returning device by:
1. Persistent device ID (preferred)
2. Device name + capabilities (fallback)
3. Any camera (if only one)

Why not just first camera?
- User may have multiple cameras
- Wrong camera would be confusing

## Overlay During Reconnect
Show subtle overlay on frozen frame:
- "Camera disconnected - reconnecting..."
- Animated spinner or dots
- Remove immediately on reconnect

## Timing Parameters
- Poll interval: 2 seconds
- Active poll duration: 30 seconds
- Background poll: Every 10 seconds (indefinitely)

## State Transitions
- Capturing → Reconnecting: On device loss
- Reconnecting → Capturing: On successful reconnect
- Reconnecting → Idle: On timeout (with user notification)

## User Notification
- On disconnect: Brief overlay, no popup
- On reconnect: Overlay disappears, maybe toast
- On timeout: Notification with options ("Camera not found. [Try Again] [Settings]")

## Testing
- USB unplug/replug while capturing
- USB hub reset
- Multiple cameras, remove non-active one
- Remove and plug in different camera

title: Handle Windows sleep/wake and screensaver events
description:
Properly handle system sleep/wake cycles and screensaver activation on Windows. Camera and render state must be correctly preserved and restored.

## Events to Handle

### Power Events
- PBT_APMSUSPEND: System going to sleep
- PBT_APMRESUMEAUTOMATIC: System waking up
- PBT_APMRESUMESUSPEND: System waking (user-initiated)

### Screensaver Events
- WM_SYSCOMMAND with SC_SCREENSAVE: Screensaver activating
- Session unlock: Screensaver ended

## Registration
```c
// Power events
RegisterPowerSettingNotification(hwnd, &GUID_MONITOR_POWER_ON, 0);

// Or handle in WndProc
case WM_POWERBROADCAST:
    switch (wParam) {
        case PBT_APMSUSPEND: OnSleep(); break;
        case PBT_APMRESUMEAUTOMATIC: OnWake(); break;
    }
```

## Sleep Behavior
On sleep:
1. Pause capture (release camera)
2. Note current state
3. GPU resources may become invalid

On wake:
1. Wait briefly (USB enumeration takes time)
2. Reinitialize GPU if needed
3. Attempt to reopen camera
4. Resume capture if successful
5. If camera unavailable, show freeze frame and poll

## Screensaver Behavior
Options:
1. **Pause during screensaver**: Save power, resume after
2. **Continue during screensaver**: Waste power, but no latency on return
3. **Prevent screensaver**: Bad for power, user expectation violation

Recommendation: Option 1 (pause during screensaver)

## Session Lock Handling
When user locks screen:
- Feed still technically running (but invisible)
- Could pause to save resources
- Resume on unlock

## Timing Considerations
- Wake sequence takes 2-5 seconds
- Camera may not appear immediately
- Polling period: 500ms after wake
- Timeout: 30 seconds before giving up

## Testing
- Sleep/wake cycle (close lid, open)
- Hibernate/resume
- Screensaver activation
- Lock/unlock (Win+L)
- Fast user switching

title: Implement MJPEG and YUYV frame decoding
description:
Decode compressed or formatted frames from camera into a standard internal format (RGBA or similar) for processing. Most microscope cameras output MJPEG or YUYV.

## Common Camera Formats
| Format | Description | Decode Complexity |
|--------|-------------|-------------------|
| MJPEG | Motion JPEG (each frame is JPEG) | Hardware decode possible |
| YUYV/YUY2 | Packed YUV 4:2:2 | Simple CPU conversion |
| NV12 | Planar YUV 4:2:0 | Common on modern cameras |
| RGB24 | Raw RGB (rare for UVC) | No conversion needed |

## Decoding Requirements
- MJPEG: Decompress JPEG to RGB/RGBA
- YUYV: Convert YUV 4:2:2 to RGB/RGBA
- Prefer hardware acceleration for MJPEG
- CPU fallback for all formats
- Output consistent RGBA format for processing pipeline

## Performance Targets
- 1080p MJPEG decode: <10ms (hardware), <30ms (software)
- 1080p YUYV convert: <5ms (SIMD optimized)
- Target: Never be the latency bottleneck

## Hardware Acceleration Options
### Windows
- Media Foundation / D3D11 video decoder for MJPEG
### macOS
- VideoToolbox for hardware JPEG decode
### Linux
- VA-API or VDPAU if available
- Always have CPU fallback

## Implementation Strategy
1. Start with CPU-only (simpler, works everywhere)
2. Profile to confirm not bottleneck
3. Add hardware path if CPU decode is too slow
4. Abstract decode interface so backends are swappable

## Color Space Notes
JPEG uses YCbCr internally. Proper color space conversion matters for accurate colors. Don't just multiply - use correct BT.601 or BT.709 coefficients based on source.

title: Implement overlay compositing system
description:
Build a simple overlay system for compositing text and graphics onto frames. Supports timestamp, custom text, and potential future overlays like scale bars.

## Overlay Types (v1)

- **Custom text**: User-defined string

## Rendering Requirements
- Text must be crisp and readable
- Shadow or outline for visibility on any background
- Efficient for every-frame compositing
- Support multi-line text
- Handle long text (truncate or wrap)

## Implementation Options
### CPU Text Rendering
- Rasterize text to bitmap
- Alpha-blend onto frame
- Cache rendered text (timestamp changes every second)

### GPU Text Rendering
- Pre-rendered font atlas
- Quad per character
- More efficient for frequent updates

- Text re-render only when content changes
- Timestamp: Cache per-second, only minutes need update typically

## Future Overlay Types (Not v1)

- Logo/watermark image
- Recording indicator
- Camera name

title: EPIC: Security & Privacy
description:
Implement and verify all security and privacy requirements. Ensure the application handles camera data responsibly, maintains user trust, and follows the principle of least privilege.

## Scope
- No-network enforcement (no outbound connections)
- No-recording default (frames only in memory)
- Permission transparency UX
- Secure configuration storage
- Log sanitization (no frame data)
- Threat model documentation
- Privacy policy draft

## Success Criteria
- Network monitoring shows zero outbound connections
- Filesystem monitoring confirms no video file writes
- First-run dialog clearly explains data handling
- Config file contains no sensitive data beyond device IDs
- Logs are safe to share for debugging

## Why This Matters
Cameras are privacy-sensitive devices. Users must trust that their microscope app isn't secretly recording or transmitting data. This is especially important for laboratory users who may have proprietary/confidential work. 'Local-only, no-recording' is a core promise we must verifiably keep.

## Trust Building
- Open source (if chosen) allows audit
- Explicit documentation of what we do/don't do
- No telemetry, no analytics, no crash reporting (users can manually share logs)
- Transparency about what config stores

comments.author: Will Boudy
comments.text:
## Privacy is a Core Feature

For a camera-based application, privacy isn't optional - it's existential. Users who trust us with their camera MUST be confident we're not abusing that trust.

## The Microscope Context

Microscopes might view:
- Scientific samples (potentially proprietary research)
- Educational content (fine)
- Personal items (jewelry, collectibles)
- Documents (accidentally left on stage)

The 'accidental document' case is real - users might forget something is under the microscope. We MUST NOT capture/store/transmit this accidentally.

## Core Privacy Promises

1. **No network**: Zero connections. Not for updates, not for telemetry, not for anything.
2. **No recording**: Frames exist only in memory during display. Explicit snapshot is exception.
3. **Local only**: Everything stays on this machine.
4. **Minimal storage**: Config + logs only. Logs contain no image data.
5. **Transparent**: User can see exactly what we store.

## Verification Approach

Each release should verify these promises:
- Static analysis for network/file APIs
- Runtime monitoring during test
- Third-party audit (eventually, for high assurance)

## Privacy UX

First run: Clear, simple explanation:
'Micround displays your microscope feed on your desktop. Your video is never recorded or sent anywhere. Only you can see it.'

Settings > Privacy: Details on what's stored, how to delete everything.

title: Implement frame buffer management and pooling
description:
Design and implement efficient frame buffer management to avoid per-frame allocation and enable zero-copy paths where possible. Memory management is critical for stable long-term operation.

## Requirements
- Fixed-size buffer pool (no unbounded growth)
- Pre-allocated at startup based on resolution
- Efficient handoff between pipeline stages
- Support for GPU memory (textures) and CPU memory
- Reference counting or explicit lifetime management

## Buffer Pool Design
```
FrameBufferPool {
  capacity: usize,          // e.g., 4 frames
  frame_size: (u32, u32),   // Resolution
  format: PixelFormat,      // RGBA typically
  
  fn acquire() -> FrameBuffer  // Get free buffer
  fn release(FrameBuffer)      // Return to pool
}
```

## Ownership Model Options
### Reference Counting (Arc)
- Buffer freed when all refs dropped
- Simple API
- Risk: Refs held too long cause pool exhaustion

### Explicit Lifetime
- acquire() / release() pairs
- Compiler can't enforce, risk of leaks
- Clearer ownership semantics

Recommendation: Reference counting with timeout warning if buffer held >100ms

## Zero-Copy Paths
Ideal pipeline:
1. Camera driver writes to mapped buffer
2. GPU reads directly for processing
3. GPU writes to wallpaper surface

Reality: Platform APIs may not align. Minimize copies even if zero-copy impossible.

## Pool Sizing
- Minimum 3 frames for triple buffering
- Maximum 5-6 frames to bound memory
- At 1080p RGBA: ~8MB per frame
- 4K RGBA: ~32MB per frame
- Pool for 4K: ~160MB (acceptable)

## Memory Pressure Handling
- If pool exhausted, drop oldest frame
- Log warning when pool pressure high
- Never block producer waiting for consumer

## Testing
- Long-running test: verify no memory growth
- Pool exhaustion test: verify graceful degradation
- Buffer lifetime test: verify proper release

comments.author: Will Boudy
comments.text:
## Memory Budget Calculation

For 4K RGBA at 60fps:
- Single frame: 3840 × 2160 × 4 bytes = 33.2 MB
- Triple buffer: 99.6 MB
- With headroom (5 frames): 166 MB

This fits in the 200MB target but is tight. Consider:
- Reduce buffer count for memory-constrained systems
- Use lower internal resolution if source is lower

## Buffer Pool Implementation Notes

### Acquisition Strategy
When pool empty:
- DON'T: Block waiting (can deadlock)
- DON'T: Allocate new (breaks memory bound)
- DO: Return None/Error, let caller decide (usually drop frame)

### Release Verification
In debug builds, track buffer lifecycle:
- Timestamp on acquire
- Warn if held > 100ms
- Detect double-release

### GPU Buffer Management
If using GPU buffers:
- Different pool per GPU context
- Cross-GPU sharing is complex (avoid if possible)
- D3D11/Metal/OpenGL all have different semantics

## Fragmentation Concern

Long-running apps can fragment memory. Mitigations:
- Allocate all buffers at startup
- Use fixed-size pool (never grow/shrink at runtime)
- If resolution changes, tear down and recreate pool

title: Implement camera state management and lifecycle
description:
Manage the state machine for camera operations: discovery, selection, opening, capturing, closing, and error states. Clean state management prevents resource leaks and undefined behavior.

## Camera States
```
┌──────────────┐
│ Disconnected │ (no device)
└──────┬───────┘
       │ device_arrived
       ▼
┌──────────────┐
│   Available  │ (enumerated, not open)
└──────┬───────┘
       │ open()
       ▼
┌──────────────┐
│   Opening    │ (format negotiation in progress)
└──────┬───────┘
       │ success
       ▼
┌──────────────┐
│    Ready     │ (open, not capturing)
└──────┬───────┘
       │ start_capture()
       ▼
┌──────────────┐     capture_error
│  Capturing   │────────────────────►┌───────┐
└──────────────┘                     │ Error │
       │ stop_capture()              └───┬───┘
       ▼                                 │ recover()
┌──────────────┐◄────────────────────────┘
│    Ready     │
└──────┬───────┘
       │ close()
       ▼
┌──────────────┐
│   Available  │
└──────────────┘
```

## State Transition Rules
- Transitions must be atomic
- Invalid transitions logged as warnings
- All transitions emit events
- Resources released on exit from state

## Resource Management
- Device handle: acquired in Opening, released in close()
- Capture buffers: allocated in start_capture(), freed in stop_capture()
- Thread: started with capture, joined on stop

## Concurrency Considerations
- State changes must be thread-safe
- Public API serializes requests
- Callbacks/events fire on capture thread
- UI must handle async state updates

## Error Recovery
From Error state, options are:
1. Retry open (if device still present)
2. Return to Available (user can retry)
3. Return to Disconnected (if device gone)

title: Implement X11 root window wallpaper on Linux
description:
Render the live feed to the X11 root window for display as desktop wallpaper. This is the primary Linux approach and works across most X11-based desktop environments.

## Approach
Draw directly to the root window or create a window with desktop type hint:

### Option A: Root Window Direct
```c
Display* display = XOpenDisplay(NULL);
Window root = DefaultRootWindow(display);
// Draw to root window pixmap
```

### Option B: Desktop Window Type
```c
Atom type = XInternAtom(display, "_NET_WM_WINDOW_TYPE_DESKTOP", False);
XChangeProperty(display, window, "_NET_WM_WINDOW_TYPE", XA_ATOM, 32,
                PropModeReplace, (unsigned char*)&type, 1);
```

## Compositor Interaction
Problem: Compositors (Mutter, KWin, Picom) may paint over root window.

Solutions:
- Desktop type hint (compositor should respect)
- Work with compositor via D-Bus (DE-specific)
- Detect compositor, choose strategy

## Per-DE Considerations
### GNOME
- Uses Mutter compositor
- Desktop icons handled by Nautilus or extension
- May need to draw to Nautilus window

### KDE
- Uses KWin compositor
- Desktop handled by Plasma shell
- May need Plasma wallpaper plugin (complex)

### XFCE
- Uses Xfwm or external compositor
- xfdesktop handles desktop
- Root window approach may work

## Rendering
- XShmPutImage for fast rendering (with MIT-SHM extension)
- OpenGL to window/pixmap if available
- Fallback to XPutImage (slower)

## Testing
- Test on GNOME, KDE Plasma, XFCE
- Test with compositors enabled/disabled
- Test multi-monitor on X11
- Verify desktop icons remain interactive

title: Design first-run user experience

title: Implement crash detection and recovery state
description:

## Detection Mechanism

1. Check for 'running' marker file/flag
2. If present and app wasn't running: Crash occurred

On normal operation:
1. Write 'running' marker on startup
2. Remove marker on clean shutdown

## Marker Storage
Options:
- Separate file: micround.running
- Config file field: last_clean_shutdown = false
- PID file: If PID exists but process doesn't

Recommendation: Config file field (atomic with config save)

1. Log crash occurrence
2. Restore original wallpaper immediately
3. Clear running marker
4. Optionally: Show notification explaining recovery
5. Don't auto-restart feed (user should initiate)

## User Communication
Notification on crash recovery:
"Micround recovered from unexpected shutdown. Your original wallpaper has been restored. Click to restart the feed."

## Preventing Stuck Wallpaper
Multiple layers of protection:
1. Running marker for crash detection
2. Original wallpaper always stored before any changes
3. Platform failsafe (if possible): Register cleanup handler

## Cleanup Handler (Platform-Specific)
### Windows
- SetUnhandledExceptionFilter for crash handler
- atexit() for normal exit
- Ctrl+C handler

### macOS
- signal handlers for SIGTERM, SIGINT
- NSApplicationWillTerminate notification

### Linux
- signal handlers
- atexit()

## Testing

- Verify wallpaper restored on next launch
- Test power failure scenario (harder)

title: Define application lifecycle and state machine
description:
Document and implement the application lifecycle: startup sequence, normal operation states, shutdown sequence, and transitions between them. Clear state machine prevents race conditions and undefined behavior.

## Application States
```
                    ┌─────────────────────────────────────┐
                    │                                     │
   ┌────────┐    ┌──▼───┐    ┌────────┐    ┌─────────┐  │
   │Starting│───►│ Idle │◄──►│Running │◄──►│ Paused  │  │
   └────────┘    └───┬──┘    └────┬───┘    └─────────┘  │
                     │            │                      │
                     │       ┌────▼────┐                 │
                     │       │  Error  │─────────────────┘
                     │       └─────────┘
                     │
                ┌────▼────┐
                │Stopping │
                └────┬────┘
                     │
                ┌────▼────┐
                │  Done   │
                └─────────┘
```

## State Descriptions
- **Starting**: Initialization in progress (config load, resource allocation)
- **Idle**: Ready but not capturing (no camera selected or feed stopped)
- **Running**: Actively capturing and rendering
- **Paused**: Capture continues, display frozen
- **Error**: Recoverable error state (camera lost, etc.)
- **Stopping**: Cleanup in progress
- **Done**: Application can exit

## Transition Rules
- All transitions must be explicit and logged
- Invalid transitions should be caught and logged as bugs
- Error state should allow recovery to Idle or Running
- Stopping must complete cleanup regardless of previous state

## Startup Sequence
1. Load configuration
2. Initialize logging
3. Initialize platform abstractions
4. Restore previous state if clean shutdown, else restore wallpaper
5. Transition to Idle or Running based on settings

## Shutdown Sequence
1. Transition to Stopping
2. Stop capture
3. Restore original wallpaper
4. Persist current settings
5. Write clean shutdown marker
6. Release all resources

title: Handle Windows display configuration changes
description:
Detect and respond to display configuration changes: resolution changes, monitor connect/disconnect, arrangement changes, DPI changes. The app must adapt without crashing or requiring restart.

## Events to Handle

### WM_DISPLAYCHANGE
- Triggered when: Resolution change, display add/remove
- Response: Re-enumerate displays, resize windows

### WM_DPICHANGED
- Triggered when: DPI setting changed, window moved to different DPI display
- Response: Rescale window, adjust rendering

### Shell events
- Explorer restart: WorkerW hierarchy may be recreated
- Wallpaper change by user: Should not affect us (we're independent)

## Detection Mechanism
Register for notifications:
```c
// Direct message handling
case WM_DISPLAYCHANGE:
    OnDisplayChange(wParam, lParam);
    break;

// Or register for shell notifications
SHChangeNotifyRegister(...)
```

## Response Algorithm
```
On display change:
1. Enumerate current displays
2. Compare with known configuration
3. For each display:
   - If new: Create wallpaper window
   - If removed: Destroy corresponding window
   - If changed: Resize/reposition window
4. Rebuild WorkerW hierarchy if needed
5. Continue feed
```

## Edge Cases
- Display removed while it was the target
  → Move feed to remaining display, notify user
- All displays changed (dock/undock)
  → Full reconfiguration
- Resolution changed mid-frame
  → Abort current frame, reconfigure, continue
- DPI change on multi-DPI setup
  → Per-monitor DPI awareness required

## Per-Monitor DPI Awareness
Application manifest must declare:
- DPI awareness level (Per-Monitor V2 recommended)
- Without this, Windows lies about display sizes

## Testing

- Connect external monitor
- Disconnect monitor showing feed
- Change DPI setting
- Dock/undock laptop
- Explorer crash and restart

title: Design configuration file schema and storage

Define the configuration file format, schema, and storage location. Configuration must be human-readable, validatable, and robust against corruption.

title: Implement GPU-accelerated processing path
description:
Build GPU-accelerated versions of processing operations for efficient sustained operation. GPU processing is essential for keeping CPU usage low and enabling 60fps on integrated graphics.

- No GPU memory growth over time

- Shader compilation fail: Fall back to CPU

title: EPIC: Windows Wallpaper Backend
description:
Implement the Windows-specific wallpaper rendering backend using the WorkerW window-behind-icons approach. This is the primary target platform and must support Windows 10 (1903+) and Windows 11.

## Scope
- WorkerW/SHELLDLL_DefView hierarchy discovery
- Window creation and positioning behind desktop icons
- Direct rendering to window surface
- DWM compositor interaction
- Multi-monitor support on Windows
- Display change detection and adaptation
- Screensaver/lock screen handling

## Success Criteria
- Feed visible behind desktop icons within 1 second of start
- No flicker during normal operation
- Survives display resolution/arrangement changes
- Works on Windows 10 21H2+ and Windows 11
- Full-screen apps don't break the feed
- Returns to normal after screensaver

## Why This Matters
Windows is the primary target with the largest user base. The WorkerW approach is well-documented in the wallpaper engine community and proven to work. This is the 'reference implementation' that proves the core concept before we tackle more challenging platforms.

## Technical Notes
The WorkerW approach exploits the Windows desktop hierarchy where a hidden WorkerW window sits between the wallpaper and desktop icons. By spawning this window and rendering to it, we can display dynamic content as if it were the wallpaper. This is technically undocumented behavior but has been stable across Windows versions since 8.

title: Handle macOS camera permissions and App Nap
description:
Properly request camera permissions and prevent App Nap from throttling the background capture process.

## Camera Permission
macOS requires explicit permission for camera access:

### Info.plist
```xml
<key>NSCameraUsageDescription</key>
<string>Micround needs camera access to display your microscope feed as wallpaper.</string>
```

### Runtime Request
```swift
AVCaptureDevice.requestAccess(for: .video) { granted in
    if granted {
        // Proceed
    } else {
        // Show guidance to enable in System Preferences
    }
}
```

### Handling Denial
- Detect permission denied
- Show user-friendly message
- Direct to System Preferences > Privacy > Camera
- Re-check on app focus return

## App Nap Prevention
macOS aggressively throttles background apps. Prevent with:

```swift
ProcessInfo.processInfo.disableAutomaticTermination("Displaying live feed")
ProcessInfo.processInfo.disableSuddenTermination()

// Or use NSProcessInfo activity
activity = ProcessInfo.processInfo.beginActivity(
    options: [.userInitiated, .idleSystemSleepDisabled],
    reason: "Live microscope feed display"
)
```

## Hardened Runtime
For notarization, app must use hardened runtime:
- Camera entitlement required
- com.apple.security.device.camera

## Testing
- Fresh install: permission prompt appears
- Denied permission: helpful guidance shown
- App Nap: verify no throttling when minimized
- Verify notarization succeeds

title: Define and implement unified capture API
description:
Create the public API surface for the capture subsystem that the rest of the application uses. This API must be platform-agnostic and safe to use from any thread.

## API Design Goals
- Simple and hard to misuse
- Async-friendly (operations may take time)
- Thread-safe
- Clear ownership of frame data
- Comprehensive error information

## Proposed API Surface
```
// Discovery
fn enumerate_cameras() -> Vec<CameraDevice>
fn subscribe_device_changes(callback: Fn(DeviceEvent))

// Selection
fn select_camera(device_id: DeviceId) -> Result<CameraHandle>
fn get_selected_camera() -> Option<CameraDevice>

// Capture control
fn start_capture(settings: CaptureSettings) -> Result<()>
fn stop_capture()
fn is_capturing() -> bool

// Frame access
fn subscribe_frames(callback: Fn(Frame))
fn unsubscribe_frames()

// Settings
fn get_capabilities(device_id: DeviceId) -> Vec<CameraCapability>
fn get_current_format() -> Option<CaptureFormat>
```

## Frame Ownership
Frames delivered to subscriber must be either:
1. Owned data (subscriber receives copy)
2. Reference-counted (subscriber can hold reference)

Option 2 is more efficient but requires careful lifetime management. Start with option 1 (simpler), optimize if profiling shows it matters.

## Thread Safety
- All public methods safe to call from any thread
- Internal synchronization via mutex or channel
- Callbacks fire on capture thread (subscriber must handle)

## Error Types
- DeviceNotFound
- DeviceBusy
- FormatNegotiationFailed
- CaptureError(details)
- PermissionDenied (macOS)

## Testing Strategy
- Mock implementation for unit testing consumers
- Integration tests with real cameras
- Stress test rapid start/stop cycles

comments.author: Will Boudy
comments.text:
## API Design Goals

This is the PUBLIC interface that the rest of the application uses. Design principles:

1. **Hide complexity**: Users of this API shouldn't know about V4L2 vs Media Foundation vs AVFoundation
2. **Thread safety**: All methods safe to call from any thread
3. **Async-aware**: Long operations should not block
4. **Testable**: Mock implementation must be possible

## Frame Ownership Model

The frame delivery model has significant implications:

**Option A: Owned frames (copy)**
```rust
fn subscribe<F: Fn(Frame)>(callback: F)
// Subscriber receives owned copy
```
Pros: Simple, no lifetime complexity
Cons: Memory copy per frame, per subscriber

**Option B: Reference-counted frames**
```rust
fn subscribe<F: Fn(Arc<Frame>)>(callback: F)
// Subscriber holds reference
```
Pros: Zero-copy for read-only access
Cons: Must be careful about holding refs too long

**Recommendation**: Start with Option A (simpler), profile, switch to B if copy overhead is measurable.

## Error Granularity

Different errors need different responses:
- PermissionDenied: Show user guidance, don't retry
- DeviceBusy: Retry with backoff
- DeviceNotFound: Wait for device events
- CaptureTimeout: Single frame, ignore; multiple, escalate

Capture this in the error types.

title: Establish error handling strategy and types
description:
Define how errors are represented, propagated, and handled throughout the system. Consistent error handling is crucial for reliability and debuggability.

## Error Categories

### Recoverable Errors
- Camera temporarily unavailable
- Frame capture timeout (single frame)
- Transient render failure
→ Handling: Retry, log, continue

### User-Actionable Errors
- Camera permission denied
- No cameras found
- Selected camera removed
→ Handling: Notify user, suggest action

### Fatal Errors
- GPU driver failure
- Out of memory
- Critical resource unavailable
→ Handling: Log, restore safe state, exit gracefully

## Error Type Design
- Error enum with variants per category
- Rich context (what operation, what component)
- Chain/cause support for wrapped errors
- User-friendly messages separate from technical details

## Propagation Strategy
- Within component: Result types, early return
- Across components: Error events via message bus
- To user: Translated to actionable messages in UI

## Logging Integration
Every error should be loggable with:
- Severity level
- Component origin
- Timestamp
- Context (device ID, operation, etc.)
- Optional stack trace (debug builds)

## Anti-patterns to Avoid
- Silent failure (swallowing errors)
- Panic/crash on recoverable errors
- Exposing technical jargon to users
- Inconsistent error representations

title: Implement frame scaling engine with multiple modes
description:
Build the scaling engine that resizes camera frames to fit display dimensions. Support multiple scaling modes to give users control over how the feed fills their screen.

## Scaling Modes

### Fit (Letterbox)
- Scale to fit entirely within display bounds
- Maintain aspect ratio
- Black bars on sides or top/bottom
- No cropping, see entire frame

### Fill (Crop to Cover)
- Scale to completely cover display
- Maintain aspect ratio
- Crop overflow edges
- No black bars, may lose edges

### Stretch
- Scale to exactly match display dimensions
- Does NOT maintain aspect ratio
- No black bars, no cropping
- Image may appear distorted

### Center (No Scale)
- Display at original resolution
- Center on display
- Black bars if smaller than display
- Crop if larger than display

## Implementation Requirements
- High-quality filtering (bilinear minimum, lanczos for downscale)
- GPU-accelerated path for performance
- CPU fallback for compatibility
- Sub-pixel accurate positioning
- Efficient for every-frame operation

## Performance Targets
- 1080p → 4K upscale: <3ms GPU, <15ms CPU
- 4K → 1080p downscale: <3ms GPU, <15ms CPU
- Memory allocation: Reuse buffers, don't allocate per frame

## Algorithm Notes
- For upscaling: Bilinear is usually sufficient (frames are soft anyway)
- For downscaling: Lanczos or bicubic prevents aliasing
- Consider SIMD intrinsics for CPU path

## GPU Implementation Options
- Compute shader (most control)
- Texture sampling with hardware filtering (simplest)
- Dedicated image processing APIs (platform-specific)

## Testing
- Test all 4 modes with various aspect ratios
- Test extreme scale factors (10x up, 10x down)
- Visual inspection for artifacts
- Performance benchmarks

title: Implement camera hot-plug detection and handling
description:
Detect when cameras are connected or disconnected and respond appropriately. Essential for the 'day-30' reliability requirement where cameras may be temporarily unplugged.

## Requirements
- Detect device arrival within 2 seconds
- Detect device removal immediately
- Fire events for both arrival and removal
- Support automatic reconnection to previously-selected camera
- Don't crash or hang on hot-plug events

## Platform-Specific Approaches

### Windows
- Register for device notifications (RegisterDeviceNotification)
- WM_DEVICECHANGE messages
- Or poll device list periodically (less responsive)

### macOS
- AVCaptureDevice notifications
- NSNotification for device connect/disconnect
- IOKit for lower-level detection

### Linux
- udev monitoring (libudev or udev rules)
- inotify on /dev/video*
- Or poll /sys/class/video4linux

## Event Flow
```
Camera Plugged In:
1. OS notifies us of new device
2. Enumerate to get device details
3. Fire CameraConnected event
4. If this was the selected camera, attempt reconnect

Camera Unplugged:
1. OS notifies us (or capture fails)
2. Fire CameraDisconnected event
3. If currently capturing, handle gracefully
4. Show last frame (freeze)
5. Start reconnection polling
```

## Reconnection Logic
- Poll every 2 seconds for up to 30 seconds
- If device returns, seamlessly resume
- If timeout, notify user, continue polling in background
- Match by persistent device ID, not enumeration order

## Edge Cases
- Multiple cameras, one removed (not the active one)
- Camera removed during format negotiation
- USB hub reset (all devices briefly disappear)
- Camera removed and different camera plugged into same port

title: Create and manage wallpaper window on Windows
description:
Create the window that will display the live feed, properly positioned in the desktop hierarchy. Must handle multi-monitor scenarios and be stable through system events.

- Borderless (no title bar, no frame)
- No taskbar entry
- Correct size for target display(s)
- Positioned at display origin

## Window Creation
```c
HWND hwnd = CreateWindowEx(
    WS_EX_NOACTIVATE | WS_EX_TOOLWINDOW,
    class_name,
    "",
    WS_POPUP | WS_VISIBLE,
    x, y, width, height,
    parent_workerw,  // or NULL with SetParent

```

- WS_EX_TOOLWINDOW: Don't show in taskbar/Alt+Tab
- WS_POPUP: No decorations
- WS_VISIBLE: Show immediately

## Multi-Monitor Handling
For multiple monitors:
- Option A: One window spanning all displays
- Option B: Separate window per display
- Recommendation: One window per display (simpler, handles mixed DPI)

## Window Positioning
- Use GetMonitorInfo() for accurate bounds
- Account for monitor arrangement (non-rectangular layouts)

- Test display connect/disconnect

title: Establish privacy-by-design principles and code guidelines
description:
Before writing significant code, establish the privacy principles and coding guidelines that will ensure our privacy promises are kept.

## Core Privacy Promises (Immutable)
1. **No network connections**: The app NEVER connects to any server for any reason
2. **No video recording**: Frames exist only in memory, never written to disk (except explicit user snapshot)
3. **Local-only operation**: All data stays on user's machine

## Code Guidelines

### Forbidden APIs (must never appear in codebase)
- HTTP/HTTPS client calls
- Socket connections (except localhost for IPC if needed)
- Telemetry/analytics libraries
- Video file writing (except snapshot feature)
- Cloud storage APIs

### Required Patterns
- Frame buffers cleared after use
- No frame data in logs
- Config files contain no image data
- Logs contain no sensitive paths

## Enforcement Mechanisms
1. **Code review checklist**: Every PR checked for privacy violations
2. **Static analysis**: Grep for forbidden APIs in CI
3. **Audit logging**: Track any file writes (for verification)

## Documentation
Create PRIVACY.md documenting:
- What data we collect (device IDs, settings)
- What data we DON'T collect (video, network, telemetry)
- How to verify our claims
- How to delete all data

## Why This Must Be Early
Privacy cannot be 'added later'. It must be designed in from the start:
- Architecture decisions affect privacy
- Library choices affect privacy
- If we accidentally add network code, it's much harder to remove

This task produces guidelines that all other implementation tasks must follow.

title: EPIC: Foundation & Architecture
description:
Establish the core architectural foundation for Micround including project structure, build system, cross-platform abstractions, and the internal messaging/event system that connects all components. This epic represents the 'skeleton' upon which all other functionality is built.

## Scope
- Project scaffolding and build configuration
- Cross-platform abstraction layer design
- Internal event/message bus architecture
- Core data types and interfaces
- Error handling strategy
- Logging infrastructure foundation

## Success Criteria
- Clean compilation on Windows, macOS, Linux
- All components can communicate via well-defined interfaces
- Error handling is consistent and traceable
- Build produces distributable artifacts

## Why This Matters
Without solid architectural foundations, cross-platform development becomes a maintenance nightmare. Investing time here prevents exponential technical debt as we add OS-specific backends. The abstraction layer is the 'contract' that allows parallel development of platform backends.

comments.author: Will Boudy
comments.text:
## Foundation Philosophy

This epic establishes the 'bones' of the project. Decisions made here echo throughout development. Take time to get them right - refactoring foundations is expensive.

## Technology Decision Framework

When choosing technologies (language, frameworks, etc.), weight these factors:
1. **Performance**: Can it achieve <100ms latency? 
2. **Cross-platform**: Does it work on Windows/macOS/Linux without heroics?
3. **Maintainability**: Is the ecosystem healthy? Good docs? Active community?
4. **Development velocity**: Can we iterate quickly?

## Why Rust is Recommended (But Not Mandated)

Rust offers:
- Zero-cost abstractions (performance like C++)
- Memory safety without GC (no pauses)
- Excellent cross-platform tooling (cargo, cross)
- Strong type system (catch bugs at compile time)
- Great concurrency primitives (needed for capture threading)

Downsides:
- Steeper learning curve
- Longer initial development
- Smaller pool of contributors

Alternatives:
- **C++**: Familiar, but manual memory management, build system pain
- **Go**: Simpler, but GC pauses may impact latency
- **Python with C extensions**: Fast iteration, but performance cliff

## Architectural Principles

1. **Separation of Concerns**: Capture knows nothing about rendering
2. **Platform Abstraction**: Core logic portable, platforms in separate modules
3. **Testability**: Mock any external dependency
4. **Observability**: Log everything, measure everything
5. **Fail Gracefully**: Never crash, always recover to safe state

title: Implement camera preview in settings
description:
Display a live preview of the camera feed within the settings window so users can verify camera selection and see effect of transforms before applying.

## Preview Requirements
- Small embedded video (e.g., 320x240 or 16:9 equivalent)
- Updates at reduced framerate (10-15fps sufficient)
- Shows transforms (rotation, flip, scaling mode preview)
- Shows overlay preview
- Indicates camera status (no camera, error)

## Implementation Options
1. **Separate capture stream**: Open camera twice (one for preview, one for wallpaper)
   - Pro: Independent
   - Con: May conflict on exclusive-access cameras

2. **Shared capture with preview tap**: Fork frames to preview
   - Pro: Single camera access
   - Con: More complex routing

3. **Downscaled wallpaper copy**: Preview is just downscaled current output
   - Pro: What you see is what you get
   - Con: Only works when feed is running

Recommendation: Option 2 (shared capture) for maximum compatibility.

## Preview States
- Camera not selected: "Select a camera"
- Camera selected, not capturing: "Click preview to test"
- Capturing: Live preview
- Error: Error message with guidance

## Performance
- Preview should not impact main feed performance
- Drop preview frames if processing busy
- Use lower resolution decode if camera supports

## Integration with Settings
When user changes:
- Rotation: Preview updates
- Flip: Preview updates  
- Scaling mode: Show simulated effect (overlay guides)
- Camera: Preview switches (brief black flash acceptable)

## Testing
- Verify preview matches wallpaper output
- Test preview with transforms applied
- Test settings changes while preview running

title: Implement original wallpaper backup and restore
description:
Safely store the user's original wallpaper information so it can be restored on exit, crash, or uninstall. This is critical for user trust - we must never 'lose' their wallpaper.

## What to Store
- Path to original wallpaper image (if applicable)
- Wallpaper style/position settings
- Per-monitor wallpaper info (if different per display)
- Solid color value (if no image)

## Platform-Specific Retrieval

### Windows
```c
// Registry: HKCU\Control Panel\Desktop
// Values: Wallpaper, WallpaperStyle, TileWallpaper
// For slideshow: HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Explorer\Wallpapers
```

### macOS
```swift
// NSWorkspace.shared.desktopImageURL(for:)
// NSWorkspace.shared.desktopImageOptions(for:)
// Per-screen wallpaper
```

### Linux
- DE-specific (GNOME: gsettings, KDE: Plasma config)
- May not be reliably retrievable across all DEs
- Document limitations

## Storage
Store in config file [internal] section:
- Platform-specific format
- Multiple entries for multi-monitor

## Restore Scenarios
1. **Normal exit**: Restore on quit
2. **Crash**: Restore on next startup (detect unclean shutdown)
3. **Uninstall**: Installer should restore
4. **Feed stop**: Restore immediately

## Restore Implementation

### Windows
```c
SystemParametersInfo(SPI_SETDESKWALLPAPER, 0, wallpaper_path, SPIF_UPDATEINIFILE | SPIF_SENDCHANGE);
```

### macOS
```swift
NSWorkspace.shared.setDesktopImageURL(url, for: screen, options: options)
```

### Linux
- gsettings for GNOME
- Plasma script for KDE
- Best effort for others

## Edge Cases
- Original was slideshow: Restore slideshow settings
- Original was solid color: Restore color
- Original file was deleted: Gracefully handle, notify user

comments.author: Will Boudy
comments.text:
## Trust is Paramount

Users will place their trust in this app by letting it modify their desktop. The ABSOLUTE WORST outcome is:
- User's wallpaper is lost forever
- App crashes and leaves desktop in broken state
- Original wallpaper can't be restored

This task is about building that trust through robust backup.

## Defense in Depth

Multiple layers of protection:
1. **Store path before any changes**: First thing, always
2. **Verify backup is valid**: Can we actually restore?
3. **Atomic config writes**: Don't corrupt mid-write
4. **Crash recovery**: Next startup restores if needed

## Platform Quirks

### Windows
- Slideshow wallpaper: Need to capture all images + settings
- Solid color: No file path, just color value
- Multi-monitor: Each monitor can have different wallpaper

### macOS
- Per-space wallpaper possible
- System wallpapers may be in protected locations
- File path URL may need security-scoped bookmark

### Linux
- GNOME uses gsettings, stores as URI
- KDE uses Plasma config files
- XFCE uses xfconf or config files
- No universal method - may need to document limitations

## Failure Mode: What if original file was deleted?

If user deletes their wallpaper image while our feed is running:
- We can't restore it (file doesn't exist)
- Options: Fall back to solid color? Show warning?
- Document this limitation clearly

title: EPIC: Video Capture System
description:
Implement the video ingest layer that discovers cameras, negotiates formats, captures frames, and delivers them to the processing pipeline. This is the 'input' side of the system and must handle the full diversity of UVC cameras with their varying capabilities.

## Scope
- Camera enumeration and discovery
- UVC device interface
- Format negotiation (resolution, framerate, pixel format)
- Frame capture with minimal latency
- Device hot-plug handling
- Camera state management (open/close/error)

## Success Criteria
- Auto-detect any UVC camera within 2 seconds
- Achieve <40ms capture latency from sensor to memory
- Handle camera disconnect/reconnect gracefully
- Support resolution range from 640x480 to 4K
- Work across Windows/macOS/Linux with same API

## Why This Matters
Video capture is the entry point for all data in the system. If we can't reliably get frames from cameras with low latency, nothing else matters. UVC standardization helps, but real-world cameras have quirks that must be handled robustly.

title: EPIC: Frame Processing Pipeline
description:
Build the frame processing pipeline that transforms raw camera frames into display-ready images. This includes color space conversion, geometric transforms (scale/crop/rotate/flip), and optional overlay compositing.

## Scope
- Color space conversion (YUYV/MJPEG/etc → RGBA)
- Scaling with multiple modes (fit/fill/stretch/center)
- Rotation (0°/90°/180°/270°)
- Horizontal/vertical flip
- Overlay compositing (timestamp, custom text)
- Frame buffer management (zero-copy where possible)
- GPU acceleration path

## Success Criteria
- Process 1080p frames in <5ms on mid-range hardware
- Zero visual artifacts from scaling/rotation
- GPU path uses <15% GPU when idle desktop
- Memory usage bounded (no growth over time)
- Overlay text readable on any background

## Why This Matters
The processing pipeline is the performance-critical path. Every frame passes through here 24-60 times per second. Efficiency here directly impacts system resource usage and thermal behavior. GPU acceleration isn't optional for sustained operation.

title: Implement camera stream opening and format negotiation
description:
Implement the logic to open a camera stream with desired parameters, negotiating the best available format when exact match isn't possible.

## Requirements
- Open camera by device ID
- Request specific resolution and framerate
- Handle format negotiation (fallback if exact match unavailable)
- Prefer hardware-friendly formats (MJPEG for efficiency)
- Report actual negotiated parameters back to caller
- Handle exclusive access conflicts gracefully

## Format Priority (for microscopes)
1. MJPEG at requested resolution (hardware decode possible)
2. YUYV/YUY2 at requested resolution (common, efficient)
3. Any format at requested resolution
4. Lower resolution with same aspect ratio
5. Any available format (last resort)

- Frame timestamping for latency tracking
- Sequence numbering for drop detection
- Graceful handling of capture errors

## Latency Minimization Strategies
- Request minimum buffer count from driver (ideally 1-2)
- Use memory-mapped buffers where possible (zero-copy)
- Don't block on downstream processing (drop if needed)
- Timestamp immediately upon frame arrival

## Frame Delivery Model
Two options:
1. **Push model**: Callback invoked for each frame
2. **Pull model**: Consumer polls for next frame

Recommendation: Push model with bounded queue. If queue full, drop oldest frame (or newest, depending on use case). Never block the capture thread.

- Capture runs on dedicated thread
- Frame delivery via channel or callback
- No shared mutable state with other threads

## Error Handling
- Single frame timeout: log, continue
- Multiple consecutive failures: transition to error state
- Device removed: notify via event, stop capture

## Metrics to Track
- Frames captured count
- Frames dropped count (capture side)
- Capture latency (time from VSYNC to callback)
- Inter-frame interval (detect framerate issues)

comments.text:
## Why Soak Testing Matters

Unit tests prove code works. Integration tests prove components work together. Soak tests prove the system works OVER TIME.

Many bugs only manifest after hours of operation:
- Memory leaks (gradual, not immediate)
- File handle exhaustion
- Thread pool starvation
- Floating point error accumulation
- Timer drift
- Resource cleanup race conditions

## Real-World Scenario Modeling

The soak tests should simulate realistic usage:
- User leaves microscope running all day at work (8 hours)
- User leaves it overnight (12-16 hours)
- User runs it for days (workstation, always-on)

Events during soak:
- System sleep/wake (laptop closes/opens)
- Display changes (dock/undock)
- Camera briefly disconnects (USB hub reset)
- System load fluctuations (other apps starting)

## Success Criteria Per Test

### 24-Hour Continuous
- 0 crashes
- Memory at end ≤ 110% of memory at start
- No frame rate degradation (compare hour 1 to hour 24)
- 0 unrecoverable errors

### Sleep/Wake Cycles
- 100% recovery rate (no failures allowed)
- Recovery time ≤ 5 seconds each time

### Camera Reconnection
- 100% reconnection success within 30 seconds
- No orphaned threads/resources

## Infrastructure Investment

Soak testing requires:
- Dedicated test machines (can't use for other work during 24h test)
- Automation (can't babysit 24 hours)
- Monitoring dashboards (see metrics over time)
- Alerting (notify on failure, don't wait until end)

This is significant investment but essential for release confidence.

title: Discover and navigate WorkerW desktop hierarchy
description:
Implement the technique to find and manipulate the Windows desktop hierarchy to position a window behind desktop icons. This is the core of the Windows wallpaper approach.

## Background: Windows Desktop Architecture
The Windows desktop is a layered system:
```
┌─────────────────────────────────┐
│       Desktop Icons             │  ← SHELLDLL_DefView (top)
├─────────────────────────────────┤
│       WorkerW (our target)      │  ← Hidden window we create/use
├─────────────────────────────────┤
│       Wallpaper                 │  ← System wallpaper (bottom)
└─────────────────────────────────┘
```

## The WorkerW Trick
1. Send message to Progman to spawn WorkerW windows
2. Find the WorkerW between icons and wallpaper
3. Parent our window to this WorkerW
4. Render to our window - appears as wallpaper

## Implementation Steps
1. Find Progman window: FindWindow("Progman", NULL)
2. Send magic message: SendMessageTimeout(Progman, 0x052C, ...)
3. This spawns WorkerW windows
4. Enumerate windows to find correct WorkerW
5. Verify by checking window hierarchy
6. Create our window as child or sibling

## Finding the Right WorkerW
After spawning, there are multiple WorkerW windows. The correct one:
- Is a child of the desktop
- Contains (or is sibling to) SHELLDLL_DefView
- Is below SHELLDLL_DefView in Z-order

## Code Pattern
```c
HWND progman = FindWindow("Progman", NULL);
SendMessageTimeout(progman, 0x052C, 0, 0, SMTO_NORMAL, 1000, NULL);

HWND workerw = NULL;
EnumWindows([](HWND hwnd, LPARAM lparam) {
    HWND shell = FindWindowEx(hwnd, NULL, "SHELLDLL_DefView", NULL);
    if (shell) {
        workerw = FindWindowEx(NULL, hwnd, "WorkerW", NULL);
    }
    return TRUE;
}, 0);
```

## Risk: Undocumented Behavior
This relies on undocumented Windows internals. Risks:
- May break with Windows updates
- Behavior differs between Windows 10/11 versions
- Must test on each target version

## Testing Matrix
- Windows 10 21H2, 22H2
- Windows 11 22H2, 23H2, 24H2
- Different wallpaper types (solid color, image, slideshow)
- Multiple monitors

comments.author: Will Boudy
comments.text:
## Historical Context

The WorkerW technique was discovered by the wallpaper engine community around 2015-2016. It exploits the fact that Windows creates a hidden WorkerW window when certain conditions are met, and this window sits in the perfect Z-order position for displaying custom wallpaper content.

## The Magic Message

The hex value 0x052C is an undocumented message that tells Progman (the Program Manager, which owns the desktop) to spawn WorkerW windows. The exact behavior:
- Sent to Progman window
- Creates two WorkerW children (sometimes)
- One WorkerW is between wallpaper and SHELLDLL_DefView
- This is where we parent our window

## Risk Assessment

**Risk Level: Medium**

This technique could break with Windows updates because:
- It's undocumented (Microsoft makes no guarantees)
- Windows shell architecture could change
- Future versions might remove Progman/WorkerW

**Mitigation:**
- Test on Windows Insider builds when available
- Have graceful fallback (show error, not crash)
- Monitor wallpaper engine forums for early warnings of breakage

## Alternative: DirectComposition

If WorkerW fails, DirectComposition is a more 'official' approach but significantly more complex. Keep it as backup plan, not primary implementation.

title: Implement processing pipeline orchestration
description:
Build the orchestration layer that chains processing operations together and manages data flow from capture to render. The pipeline must be efficient, configurable, and handle dynamic settings changes.

## Pipeline Stages
```
RawFrame (from capture)
    │
    ▼
┌─────────────┐
│   Decode    │  (if compressed format)
└─────────────┘
    │
    ▼
┌─────────────┐
│   Scale     │  (fit/fill/stretch/center)
└─────────────┘
    │
    ▼
┌─────────────┐
│  Transform  │  (rotate, flip)
└─────────────┘
    │
    ▼
┌─────────────┐
│  Overlay    │  (timestamp, text)
└─────────────┘
    │
    ▼
ProcessedFrame (to render)
```

## Configuration
Each stage configurable:
- Decode: Format-specific settings
- Scale: Mode, target dimensions
- Transform: Rotation angle, flip flags
- Overlay: Enabled, content, position

Settings changes should:
- Apply immediately (no restart)
- Not cause frame glitches
- Be validated before applying

## Threading Model
Options:
1. **Single-threaded**: Process on capture callback thread
2. **Dedicated thread**: Capture → queue → process thread → queue → render
3. **Thread pool**: Parallel frame processing

Recommendation: Option 2 (dedicated thread) for predictable latency. Option 3 unnecessary unless targeting >60fps.

## Frame Timing
- Track time spent in each stage
- Emit metrics for latency analysis
- Detect slow stages for optimization

## Dynamic Pipeline
Some stages can be skipped:
- No decode if camera outputs RGB
- No scale if resolution matches
- No transform if 0° and no flip
- No overlay if disabled

Optimize by skipping no-op stages.

## Drop Policy
If processing can't keep up:
- Drop frames at intake (newest or oldest)
- Never queue unboundedly
- Log drop rate
- Alert if drop rate exceeds threshold

## Testing
- Settings change mid-stream
- All combinations of stage configurations
- Performance profiling per stage
- Drop behavior under load

title: Implement internal event/message bus
description:
Build the internal messaging system that allows components to communicate without tight coupling. This enables the UI to send commands to subsystems and receive events without direct dependencies.

## Requirements
- Synchronous command dispatch (UI → component)
- Asynchronous event notification (component → UI)
- Type-safe message definitions
- No unbounded queues (backpressure or drop policy)
- Thread-safe (components may run on different threads)

## Message Categories
### Commands (UI → Components)
- StartCapture, StopCapture
- PauseDisplay, ResumeDisplay
- UpdateSettings
- TakeSnapshot
- SelectCamera, SelectDisplay

### Events (Components → UI)
- CameraConnected, CameraDisconnected
- CaptureStarted, CaptureStopped
- FrameDropped
- ErrorOccurred
- SettingsChanged

## Design Options
1. **Channel-based**: Typed channels per message type
2. **Bus pattern**: Central dispatcher with subscriptions
3. **Callback registration**: Direct function callbacks

## Recommendation
Channel-based for commands (direct, typed), bus pattern for events (one-to-many). Keep it simple - this isn't a distributed system.

## Anti-patterns to Avoid
- Global mutable state for 'current settings'
- Direct component references across layers
- Blocking calls that could deadlock

title: Implement Direct3D rendering to wallpaper window
description:
Set up Direct3D 11 rendering to the wallpaper window for efficient GPU-accelerated frame display. D3D11 provides the best balance of compatibility and performance on Windows.

## D3D11 Setup Requirements
1. Create D3D11 device and context
2. Create swap chain for our window
3. Set up render target view
4. Configure present parameters for low latency

## Device Creation
```c
D3D_FEATURE_LEVEL levels[] = { D3D_FEATURE_LEVEL_11_0 };
D3D11CreateDeviceAndSwapChain(
    NULL,                    // Adapter (NULL = default)
    D3D_DRIVER_TYPE_HARDWARE,
    NULL,                    // Software module
    flags,                   // Debug flags if debug build
    levels, 1,
    D3D11_SDK_VERSION,
    &swapChainDesc,
    &swapChain,
    &device,
    &featureLevel,
    &context
);
```

## Swap Chain Configuration
- Buffer count: 2 (double buffer)
- Format: DXGI_FORMAT_B8G8R8A8_UNORM
- Swap effect: DXGI_SWAP_EFFECT_FLIP_DISCARD (low latency)
- Windowed: TRUE
- Sample count: 1 (no MSAA needed for video)

## Frame Presentation
For each frame:
1. Get processed frame from pipeline (as texture or CPU buffer)
2. Copy to back buffer (or map directly if possible)
3. Present(1, 0) for vsync, Present(0, 0) for immediate

## Latency Optimization
- Use FLIP model swap chain
- Consider SetMaximumFrameLatency(1)
- Don't use DXGI_PRESENT_DO_NOT_WAIT unless measuring
- Vsync tradeoff: Tearing vs latency

## Resize Handling
On window resize (display change):
1. Release render target view
2. ResizeBuffers() on swap chain
3. Recreate render target view

## Error Handling
- Device lost: Full recreation
- Out of memory: May need to reduce resolution
- Present errors: Log and retry

## Integration with Processing Pipeline
Frame handoff options:
1. CPU buffer → ID3D11Texture2D via UpdateSubresource
2. Shared texture directly from processing (zero-copy)
3. Cross-adapter texture sharing (multi-GPU)

Start with option 1, optimize to 2 if needed.

## Testing
- Verify stable framerate
- Test display change during render
- Test GPU driver crash/recovery
- Test on integrated vs dedicated GPU

title: Design user-facing error messages and recovery guidance
description:
Design the messages users see when things go wrong, and the guidance that helps them fix problems. Good error UX is the difference between user frustration and user confidence.

## Error Message Design Principles

1. **Tell users what happened** (in plain language)
2. **Tell users what to do** (specific action)
3. **Don't blame the user**
4. **Don't use technical jargon**

## Error Scenarios and Messages

### Camera Errors

| Situation | Bad Message | Good Message |
|-----------|-------------|--------------|
| Camera not found | 'Device enumeration failed: HRESULT 0x80070002' | 'No camera detected. Connect your USB microscope and click Refresh.' |
| Camera in use | 'ERROR_SHARING_VIOLATION' | 'Camera is being used by another app. Close other apps using the camera and try again.' |
| Permission denied | 'Access denied' | 'Camera access needed. Click here to open Privacy settings and allow Micround to use your camera.' |

### Display Errors

| Situation | Good Message |
|-----------|--------------|
| Display disconnected | 'The display showing your feed was disconnected. Feed moved to [Primary Display].' |
| Resolution changed | 'Display resolution changed. Adjusting feed...' (no action needed) |

### Feed Errors

| Situation | Good Message |
|-----------|--------------|
| Feed frozen | 'Feed appears frozen. [Restart Feed]' |
| Camera disconnected mid-feed | 'Camera disconnected. Waiting to reconnect...' → 'Camera not found. [Try Again] [Select Different Camera]' |

## Recovery Actions
Every error should have:
- Clear next step (button or instruction)
- Way to dismiss if user wants to ignore
- Link to help/troubleshooting if complex

## Tone
- Friendly but not cute
- Confident but not dismissive
- Helpful but not condescending

## Implementation Notes
- Store message templates in one place (localization-ready)
- Include error code for support purposes (small, optional 'Details')
- Log full technical error internally
- Show simple message to user

## Testing
- Trigger each error condition
- Verify message is helpful
- Get user feedback on clarity

Implement camera capture using Windows Media Foundation API. This is the modern Windows API for video capture (DirectShow is legacy). Must enumerate devices, negotiate formats, and capture frames with low latency.

## Media Foundation Capture Flow
1. Create IMFMediaSource from device
2. Configure IMFSourceReader
3. Set output media type (prefer NV12 or MJPEG)
4. Read samples in loop via ReadSample()

## Key APIs
- MFEnumDeviceSources for enumeration
- IMFSourceReader for capture
- IMFMediaType for format negotiation

## Testing
- Test with built-in webcams
- Test with USB microscopes
- Test format negotiation fallbacks

title: Design and document core data types and interfaces
description:
Define the fundamental data types and interfaces that all components will use. These are the 'contracts' between system layers and must be carefully designed before implementation begins.

## Key Types to Define

### Frame Types
- RawFrame: As captured from camera (format-tagged)
- ProcessedFrame: Ready for display (RGBA)
- FrameMetadata: Timestamp, sequence, source device

### Device Types
- CameraDevice: Enumerated camera with capabilities
- DisplayInfo: Monitor geometry, DPI, identifier
- DeviceId: Persistent identifier for cameras

### Configuration Types
- UserSettings: All user-configurable options
- AppState: Runtime state (running, paused, error)
- TransformSettings: Scale mode, rotation, flip

### Command/Event Types
- Command: Actions from UI to components
- Event: Notifications from components to UI

## Interface Boundaries
1. Capture → Processing: Frame handoff
2. Processing → Render: Processed frame delivery
3. UI ↔ All: Commands and events
4. Config ↔ All: Settings read/write

## Why Careful Design Matters
Changing interfaces after implementation is expensive. Getting the Frame types right is especially critical - they're touched by every component on every frame. Over-engineering here is preferable to constant refactoring later.

## Interface Stability Principle

These interfaces will be used throughout the codebase. Once implementation begins in earnest, changes become expensive. Spend time here to get it right.

## Frame Type Design Considerations

### Zero-Copy Potential
Design Frame types to support zero-copy where possible:
- Use reference-counted smart pointers
- Avoid unnecessary cloning
- Consider memory-mapped buffer references

### Pixel Format Handling
Support multiple pixel formats but standardize early:
- Input: MJPEG, YUYV, NV12, RGB24 (whatever cameras send)
- Internal: RGBA8 (standard, GPU-friendly)
- Don't convert until necessary

### Timestamp Precision
Use monotonic clock, not wall clock:
- Monotonic survives system time changes
- Use nanoseconds for latency measurement precision
- Wall clock only for user-facing timestamps (overlays)

## Error Type Philosophy

Errors should be:
- Typed (not just strings)
- Contextual (what operation failed, with what input)
- Recoverable vs Fatal distinction clear
- Serializable (for logging)

Don't over-engineer, but plan for structured error handling from the start.
